reference.source: Clinical medical genetics and ciliopathy references
clinicalPearls: Sensenbrenner syndrome is an autosomal recessive skeletal ciliopathy caused by defects in intraflagellar transport, most often in genes such as IFT122, WDR35, IFT43, WDR19 and IFT52.
The craniofacial hallmark is dolichocephaly from sagittal craniosynostosis, with frontal bossing, a broad forehead and low-set ears.
Ectodermal features include sparse, slow-growing fine hair, small widely spaced or hypoplastic teeth (microdontia), nail dysplasia and dry skin.
Skeletal features comprise a narrow thorax, short limbs (rhizomelic shortening), brachydactyly and short stature.
Progressive chronic kidney disease from a nephronophthisis-like tubulointerstitial nephropathy is a major cause of morbidity and can progress to end-stage kidney failure.
Hepatic fibrosis, retinal dystrophy and, in some, cardiac defects extend the multisystem ciliopathy picture and overlap with other short-rib/IFT disorders.
The narrow thorax may cause respiratory insufficiency in infancy, an important early determinant of outcome.
As a ciliopathy it overlaps clinically with Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy and other short-rib disorders, so molecular testing is key.
reference.pathophysiology: Sensenbrenner syndrome is a genetically heterogeneous ciliopathy caused by biallelic variants in genes encoding components of the intraflagellar transport (IFT) machinery, particularly the retrograde IFT-A complex (IFT122, WDR35/IFT121, IFT43, WDR19/IFT144) and, in some, the anterograde or core apparatus (IFT52). Intraflagellar transport moves protein cargo bidirectionally along the axoneme of primary cilia, and the IFT-A complex mediates retrograde transport back to the cell body and is required for normal ciliary assembly, structure and signalling. Because primary cilia coordinate developmental signalling pathways (including hedgehog signalling) in bone, ectoderm, kidney, liver and retina, disruption of IFT produces a pleiotropic disorder: abnormal cranial suture and skeletal patterning, defective ectodermal derivatives, and progressive fibrotic damage in the kidney (a nephronophthisis-like tubulointerstitial process) and liver. The specific gene and variant severity influence which systems dominate, explaining the phenotypic overlap with other IFT-related skeletal ciliopathies.
additionalDifferentials: Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy (short-rib thoracic dysplasia)
additionalInvestigations: Renal function tests and urinalysis with monitoring for progressive tubulointerstitial nephropathy
Renal ultrasound for cyst formation and echogenicity
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging for fibrosis
Skeletal survey and cranial imaging to define craniosynostosis and thoracic dimensions
Ophthalmological assessment including electroretinography for retinal dystrophy
Molecular genetic testing of an IFT/ciliopathy gene panel
redFlags: Respiratory insufficiency from a narrow thorax in infancy
Declining kidney function or signs of established kidney failure
Progressive hepatic dysfunction or portal hypertension
Progressive visual loss from retinal dystrophy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of thoracic and renal involvement: neonatal respiratory insufficiency and progressive chronic kidney disease progressing to end-stage failure are the main threats to life, whereas milder cases may reach adulthood with supportive and organ-specific management.
pitfalls: Treating the craniosynostosis in isolation and missing the underlying multisystem ciliopathy, including silent early kidney disease.
Not monitoring renal and hepatic function longitudinally, as involvement can be progressive and initially asymptomatic.
Confusing it with Ellis-van Creveld or Jeune syndrome without molecular confirmation given the overlapping skeletal features.
Overlooking retinal dystrophy that may only be detected on formal ophthalmological testing.
Underestimating respiratory risk from the narrow thorax in infancy.
references: Standard textbooks of clinical genetics and dysmorphology
Peer-reviewed reviews of skeletal ciliopathies and intraflagellar transport disorders
management: Provide multisystem supportive management of this intraflagellar-transport ciliopathy, for which no curative therapy exists
Arrange surgical correction of sagittal craniosynostosis to relieve raised intracranial pressure and allow brain growth
Support the narrow thorax with respiratory care, treating neonatal respiratory insufficiency intensively
Manage the nephronophthisis-like tubulointerstitial nephropathy and its progression, with renal replacement therapy for end-stage kidney disease
Undertake surveillance for hepatic fibrosis, retinal dystrophy with electroretinography, and cardiac defects with echocardiography, alongside dental and ectodermal supportive care
Coordinate multidisciplinary input across clinical genetics, nephrology, craniofacial surgery, and ophthalmology
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
